expectations.text: Claude identifies that manager motivation was measured after the treatment and therefore may be a mediator on the training → motivation → performance causal path
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly identifies this: 'Manager motivation level, measured one month after the training ended, sits on the causal pathway between the training and the performance outcome. It is not a pre-treatment confounder — it is a mediator (or at minimum, a post-treatment variable influenced by the treatment).' A causal diagram is also provided showing Training Program --> Manager Motivation (1 mo. post) --> Team Performance (6 mo. post).

expectations.text: Claude warns that controlling for a post-treatment mediator blocks the causal mechanism you're trying to measure, biasing the estimated training effect toward zero
expectations.evidence: The response states: 'When you condition on a mediator, you block the indirect pathway through which the treatment operates' and lists 'Coefficient on treatment is biased downward (or toward zero), because you've absorbed some of the treatment's actual effect into the mediator.' The summary reinforces: 'Including it as a control variable will attenuate your treatment effect estimate and produce a biased answer to your research question.'

expectations.text: Claude distinguishes the total effect of training (including the motivation pathway) from the direct effect (net of motivation) — and clarifies which one is typically the policy-relevant quantity
expectations.evidence: A table explicitly distinguishes total effect, direct effect, and indirect effect with corresponding correct approaches. The response clarifies: 'If your goal is simply "did the training program improve performance?", you want the total effect, and you should not condition on motivation.' The direct effect is defined as 'the effect of training, not through motivation' requiring mediation analysis.

expectations.text: Claude does NOT recommend including post-treatment motivation as a control without raising this structural concern
expectations.evidence: The response opens with 'No — this is almost certainly a bad idea, and doing so would likely bias your causal estimate.' The structural concern (mediator overcontrol) is raised immediately and is the central thesis of the entire response. No recommendation to include motivation as a control is made anywhere.

eval_feedback.overall: The response is an excellent treatment of the mediator overcontrol problem. It correctly identifies post-treatment motivation as a likely mediator, explains overcontrol bias and its direction (attenuation toward zero), clearly distinguishes total vs. direct vs. indirect effects, and unambiguously recommends against including post-treatment motivation as a covariate. The response also goes beyond the minimum by naming the 'bad control' literature (Angrist & Pischke; Cinelli, Forney & Pearl), explaining collider risks, and offering concrete alternatives including pre-treatment motivation as a valid baseline covariate. All four assertions pass with strong, direct evidence.
